```text
Peak Poker Performance

   ♠ Notice while you are doing this that part of you is thinking while
       another part of you is able to observe the thoughts.


   The purpose of this task is to help you see that thoughts come and go
very rapidly. It also shows you that you can be an observer of your
thoughts, which are just mental events. By experiencing them in this way,
you can start relating to them differently.

Acceptance: An Antidote for Resistance
Hayes recommends that we practice acceptance as a critical part of de-
fusing ourselves from our emotional difficulties. When we accept them,
we open up and make room for painful feelings, sensations, urges, and
emotions. Essentially, you drop the struggle with them, and you allow
them to be as they are. If you fight, resist, try to run from, or get over-
whelmed by them, they have the power to take you down a path you
don’t want. Instead, open up to them and let them be. This doesn’t mean
that you like them or want them – rather you just let them be.
   Tommy Angelo shared a similar sentiment on the podcast when he
shared his thoughts on where tilt originates from:

      What is the cause of suffering? The word suffering is used in
      Buddhism as a translation of an old word. It’s kind of unfortu-
      nate. A closer translation I think is just “dissatisfaction.” We all
      carry this dissatisfaction around with us all the time. We want
      things to be different than they are, or we want things to stay
      the same. And neither of those things ever happens. Nothing
      is different than it actually is, and nothing stays the same. And
      that’s why all of us carry around this fundamental undercur-
      rent of dissatisfaction. And so at the very deepest level, that’s
      the cause of all tilt, all anger, all unhappiness, and all envy. Pick
      any word that describes a negative feeling that humans have,
      and it all comes from this basic discord between reality as it is
      and reality as we wish it was.
```

```text
                                             Transform Your Mental Game

    Kristin Neff wrote a book called Self-Compassion in which she reiter-
ates Angelo’s message. She says that suffering can be explained by the
following equation:


         Suffering = Pain x Resistance


   Let’s say that you experience the pain of losing a pot or of running bad
over an extended period of time. Neff’s equation indicates that when you
resist your reality, by cursing the poker gods or in any other fashion, you
increase your suffering exponentially. She says when bad things happen, it
is what it is. Why would you want to make it worse? Her recommenda-
tion: take a few deep breaths, appreciate that you play a game for a living
(or that you have a hobby for which you have the capacity to make
money), and accept the reality of the situation. If you get too caught up in
resistance, you’ll devolve instead of evolve – the exact opposite of what
you want.
   So there you have it. When we get caught up in our thoughts and feel-
ings and resist reality, we are setting ourselves up for a lot of dissatisfac-
tion and mental game problems!

Is it Workable?
From Dr. Hayes’ perspective, the most important question to ask yourself
about your mental game is whether what you are doing (or thinking) is
workable. Is what you are doing working to make your life rich, full, and
meaningful? If it is, it’s workable, and there is no need to change it. If it is
not, it is unworkable, and you need to consider alternatives that work
better. Don’t focus on whether or not your thoughts and emotions are
true or false or good or bad, but only on whether they are workable.
    Here are a few more questions you can ask yourself to determine the
utility of your thoughts:

   ♠ Is this thought in any way helpful or useful?
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

   ♠ How could this thought or belief be helpful?
   ♠ Does having this thought or belief help me take effective action?
   ♠ Does having this thought or belief encourage me to make good
       choices?
   ♠ Am I going to trust what my mind is telling me or go with what my
       experience knows is the right thing to do?


   Suppose you make a bad read and lose a significant pot. If you are like
most players, a number of self-critical thoughts will immediately come to
mind. Maybe you spend a few minutes chastising yourself for your mis-
take. Take a moment and consider whether letting this line of thinking
guide your behavior will help you create a better more successful playing
experience. Does holding onto these thoughts help you be the player you
wish to be and do the things you want to do? Do they motivate you or
make you play better?
   If after examining your thoughts you find them to be helpful, pay at-
tention to them. If they are not, defuse them by detaching yourself from
them. Usually, negative thinking is not helpful or motivating, and it only
makes us play worse. Practicing defusion allows you to perceive these
thoughts as just bits of language, words, or pictures and not as an objec-
tive fact or the truth. Ask yourself non-judgmentally if what you are
thinking or feeling is working to give you the game that you want. You
don’t need to judge your thoughts as irrational or dysfunctional or get
into debates about whether they are true or false. Instead just ask, “Does
holding tightly to these thoughts help me achieve what I want in poker?”
   There are numerous defusion techniques which you can practice. You
can defuse a thought by thanking your mind for providing it. A simple
“thanks for sharing” will often do the trick. Another method is to distance
yourself from the thought by putting the words to a silly voice or a silly
song. Finally, you can step back and ask yourself, “How am I seeing this
situation? How am I thinking and feeling about it?” You can go one step
further and ask, “How else could I see this situation that might be more
```

```text
                                            Transform Your Mental Game

useful or helpful?” If all else fails, turn to, “What can I learn from this ex-

   Your goal is not to get rid of unhelpful thoughts, because as we have
already discussed, thought suppression does not work. Your goal is to dis-
tance yourself from them in a non-judgmental, dispassionate way. In do-
ing so, they will usually subside all on their own.
   When we interviewed him, Angelo told us that he practices observing
thoughts in a similar manner:

      Taking time every day to sit quietly and practice observing
      your thoughts is not an easy thing to do. Because a thought
      comes up, and you have to say to yourself, okay I’m now
      thinking about what an asshole my brother is. And then you
      have to go to the next level, and say I’m just going to let that
      fall aside and go back to my breathing or go back to my pos-
      ture. By doing that over and over and over, the idea is that
      when you’re at the poker table and you lose with a set and
      your mind is going crazy, that you can rise up to a higher level
      of consciousness and look down on those thoughts and say
      okay, right now my mind is temporarily insane because it’s re-
      sisting reality. The act of doing that observation, in and of it-
      self, just pulls the rug right out from the pain. At least, tempo-
      rarily. It may only be half a second, but that act of observing
      over and over and over, hundreds and thousands of times, is
      the process of using mindfulness to reduce suffering.

downswings to be lived through, and, of course, bad beats.
```

```text
Peak Poker Performance

tion that causes an emotional reaction, our attention automatically turns
inward to our thoughts and feelings. We can easily lose focus and as a re-
sult start to play poorly. Mindfulness can correct this strong tendency and
help us keep our focus where it needs to be – on the game.

Managing Impulses and Urges
A major problem with negative thoughts and feelings is that we can give in
to the impulses and urges that tend to come along with them. For example,
when we are down a buy-in, we might have the urge to gamble it up to
make our money back. Or when we’ve been running bad, we might give in
to the urge to book a small win and leave a juicy game prematurely. Feel-
ings of over-confidence or even boredom can impact our decisions.
    Generally speaking, impulsivity is characterized by a tendency to act
without thinking. Impulsivity can be to blame when we lose focus, react
instantaneously, and otherwise act in ways that we later regret. There is
some research that suggests that learning to be more mindful is associ-
ated with being more in control of one’s behavior, because if we have a
well-trained “observer” we can override thoughts and feelings and resist
temptations. Having the mental ability to be aware of your experience
and to notice urges and impulses without having to act on them is a major
advantage at the poker table. Besides practicing mindfulness away from
the table, it is a great idea to use mindfulness to help you notice and dis-
rupt urge behaviors in the moment. To do this you want to mindfully ob-
serve your problematic behavior in great detail. Pay particular attention to
the thoughts and feelings that are present when you feel a strong impulse
to make a poor choice. Many times just putting your attention spotlight
on a potential impulsive behavior will disrupt it. Realize that urges come
and go and that by being aware and accepting this fact, you become less
likely to let them affect you negatively.
    Mindfulness teaches that our present moment experience is imperma-
nent. Urges and impulses subside on their own in a matter of time, just as
thoughts and feelings do.
```

```text
                                           Transform Your Mental Game

The Challenge of Boredom
Sometimes poker players complain to me that they do impulsive things
when they feel bored. Perhaps you’ve experienced the boredom of being
card dead. Or maybe you find live events slow and tortuous. Whatever
the case, most players do not enjoy the feeling of being bored. To get
over it, many players look for spots to get involved no matter how mar-
ginal. It is very difficult to do nothing, because most of us live in a world
where our brains are constantly being over-stimulated.
   You can use mindfulness techniques to help you deal with any boredom
you experience. Notice the thoughts and feelings that you are having and
bring any urges to act to the forefront of your mind. Acknowledge and
accept that you can have these thoughts and feelings without acting on
them. This will make you less likely to react to them. Once you have man-
aged your experience of boredom successfully you can think about what
effective actions you can take. This could be a great time to pay more at-
tention to table dynamics so that you can find profitable spots later on.
   As you have probably already figured out, it is not negative emotions
that cause us a problem but what we choose to do with them that
counts. It can be helpful to make some plans in advance of behaviors you
will undertake when you are confronted with feelings like anger or bore-
dom. Use mindfulness techniques to learn about when you are most “at
risk” and have a clear idea of what actions you are committed to taking
during those times.

Summary
Most of our mental game issues actually originate from just a few
sources:

   ♠ We can be in a state of fusion, where we are so entangled in our
       thoughts that they dominate our awareness and have a huge
       influence over our behavior.
   ♠ We can try to avoid psychological pain by engaging in experiential
       avoidance. We try to escape from, get rid of, or avoid unwanted
```

```text
       impulsive and reactive as opposed to mindful, considered, and
       purposeful.


   If you want to play your A game more often, you should train yourself

   ♠ psychologically present
   ♠ in touch with your values
   ♠ able to make room for the inevitable pain of poker
   ♠ able to defuse from unhelpful thoughts, beliefs, and memories
   ♠ able to take effective action in the face of emotional discomfort
   ♠ able to fully engage in what you are doing no matter how you are
```

```text
Chapter Highlights
   ♠ Emotional hijackings are strongly correlated with high levels of
       arousal, intense emotions, and an inability to focus and think
       clearly.
   ♠ Emotional awareness is the first step to optimizing your mind.
   ♠ Emotions cause action tendencies, but those are tendencies not
       commands. You can choose how to respond.
   ♠ There are three phases to the tilt response, which our brain and
       body flow through.
   ♠ Biology plays a major role in emotional upsets or tilt responses.
   ♠ Emotional intelligence helps you identify and manage your
       emotions, and to identify the emotions of your opponents so you
       may use the information to your advantage.
   ♠ Psychological flexibility can be gained through becoming more
       present or mindful.
   ♠ Mindfulness helps to improve focus, decrease stress, increase
       self-awareness, and allow us to be more in control of our moment
       to moment behavior.
   ♠ Defusion is stepping back and separating from or detaching from
       our thoughts, images, and memories.
```
